definitions.definition: The first noble truth: birth, ageing, illness, death, union with the disliked, separation from the liked, not getting what one wants — in brief the five aggregates of clinging (SN 56.11); also one of the three marks, applying to all formations (AN 3.136).

equivalents.note: same word; Sāṃkhya and Yoga also begin from duḥkha, with a different account of its cause and end

definitions.definition: The second noble truth: craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust — craving for sensual pleasures, for becoming and for non-becoming (SN 56.11).

The third noble truth: the remainderless fading away and cessation of craving, its giving up and release (SN 56.11); by extension the cessation of each link of dependent origination, and the attainment of cessation (saññāvedayitanirodha).

notes: Same slug as the Yoga term (citta-vṛtti-nirodha); this entry adds the early-Buddhist sense.

definitions.definition: The fourth noble truth, the way leading to the cessation of suffering: the noble eightfold path (SN 56.11; SN 45.8); in the commentaries also the supramundane path-moment of each of the four stages.

equivalents.note: same word; in Buddhist usage specifically the noble eightfold path

definitions.definition: The four noble truths (suffering, its origin, its cessation, the path), to be respectively fully understood, abandoned, realised and developed (SN 56.11); what the Buddha declared because it is beneficial (SN 56.31).

literal: noble truth; truth for the noble ones

definitions.definition: Right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration (SN 45.8), the middle way that avoids sensual indulgence and self-mortification (SN 56.11); grouped into the trainings of virtue, concentration and wisdom (MN 44).

The practice that avoids the two extremes of devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification (SN 56.11); also the teaching 'by the middle' that avoids 'all exists' and 'all does not exist' through dependent origination (SN 12.15).

Impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha) and not-self (anattā): 'all formations are impermanent, all formations are suffering, all phenomena are not-self' (AN 3.136; Dhp 277–279); the term tilakkhaṇa itself is commentarial.
Arising and passing away; the first mark of all formations (AN 3.136); from the impermanence of the aggregates follows their being suffering and not fit to be taken as self (SN 22.59).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: What is not a self nor belonging to a self: each aggregate is not-self, since it leads to affliction and cannot be commanded (SN 22.59); 'all phenomena (sabbe dhammā) are not-self' (AN 3.136; Dhp 279); seeing 'this is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self' (MN 22).

equivalents.note: same word; the Buddhist Sanskrit form

definitions.definition: In ordinary usage the reflexive 'oneself' (Dhp 160); as a doctrine, a self that would be permanent, controllable and 'mine' — the suttas examine every candidate (the aggregates, feeling, consciousness, the world) and find none (MN 22; DN 15; MN 148).

equivalents.note: the same word; what the Upaniṣadic traditions affirm as ātman the suttas examine and do not find; Theravāda rejects the identification

definitions.definition: What would belong to a self; since neither self nor what belongs to self is found as true and established, views of self are foolish (MN 22; SN 35.85).
A doctrine or theory of self; clinging to it (attavādupādāna) is the fourth kind of clinging (MN 11; SN 12.2).
The five aggregates — form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness — whatever of each is past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle (SN 22.48).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: The aggregates as affected by the effluents and subject to clinging (SN 22.48); in brief, they are suffering (SN 56.11) and identity (sakkāya) (MN 44).
The first aggregate: the four great elements and form derived from them (SN 12.2); also the visible object of the eye, and the fine-material sphere of the jhānas.
Pleasant, painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of the six kinds of contact (SN 12.2); the second aggregate; the uninstructed adds a 'second dart' of mental pain (SN 36.6).
The third aggregate: perception of forms, sounds, odours, tastes, tangibles and mental objects; perceptions arise and cease with causes, some through training (DN 9).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: The fourth aggregate (volition towards the six objects); in dependent origination the bodily, verbal and mental formations conditioned by ignorance (SN 12.2); in the widest sense everything conditioned ('all saṅkhāras are impermanent'); bodily formation is breathing, verbal formation applied and sustained thought, mental formation perception and feeling (MN 44).

equivalents.note: same word; in Yoga and Vedānta primarily a latent impression, in the suttas volitional forming and everything formed

definitions.definition: The fifth aggregate: the six classes of consciousness, each reckoned by its condition as a fire by its fuel (MN 38); dependently arisen, not a self that transmigrates (MN 38); conditioned by and conditioning name-and-form (DN 15; SN 12.67).

equivalents.note: same word; the suttas deny it a permanent nature

definitions.definition: 'Consciousness non-manifesting, infinite, radiant all round', where the elements and name-and-form find no footing and cease (DN 11; MN 49); read by the commentaries as nibbāna.

Feeling, perception, volition, contact and attention (name) and the four elements and derived form (form) (SN 12.2); conditions and is conditioned by consciousness like two sheaves of reeds (SN 12.67).
The six internal (eye … mind) and six external (forms … mental objects) bases, 'the all' (SN 35.23); also the formless 'spheres' and 'that sphere' of Ud 8.1.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind as internal bases; the fifth link of dependent origination (SN 12.2).
'The all' is simply the twelve sense bases; one who would describe another all speaks beyond his domain (SN 35.23).

The four (or six: with space and consciousness) elements of which a person consists (MN 140; MN 62); the eighteen elements of sense, object and consciousness; also 'element' as in nibbāna-element and 'that element stands' (SN 12.20).
Earth (solidity), water (cohesion), fire (heat), air (motion), internal and external, each seen 'this is not mine' (MN 28; MN 62).
Whatever is hard and solid, internal (hair, nails, bones …) or external; simply the earth element, not self (MN 28, MN 62, MN 140).

The twelvefold arising of suffering from ignorance through formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming and birth to ageing-and-death, and its cessation (SN 12.1); 'whoever sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma' (MN 28).

equivalents.note: same doctrine under its Sanskrit name

definitions.definition: The phenomena that arise dependently (ageing, birth … ignorance), impermanent, conditioned, subject to cessation (SN 12.20).

The principle 'when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises; when this does not exist, that does not come to be' (SN 12.21), which stands whether or not Tathāgatas arise (SN 12.20).
The fixed course of things — dependent origination and the three marks — which stands whether Tathāgatas arise or not; a Tathāgata discovers and reveals it (SN 12.20; AN 3.136).
The natural course of things; 'it is the norm' for a bodhisatta (DN 14) and for the stages of the path to follow one another without volition (AN 10.2).
Not knowing suffering, its origin, its cessation and the way (SN 12.2); the first link of dependent origination, the last fetter and one of the effluents; it has the effluents as its origin (MN 9).

equivalents.note: same word; in the suttas not knowing the four truths, not a cosmic power or the locus of an illusory world as in Advaita

definitions.definition: The meeting of sense faculty, object and consciousness, condition for feeling (MN 18; SN 12.2); one of the four nutriments (MN 9).

Craving for sensual pleasures, for becoming and for non-becoming, which leads to renewed existence (SN 56.11); the six classes of craving for the six objects (SN 12.2); the taking up of the burden (SN 22.22).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: Craving for continued existence, one of the three cravings (SN 56.11); those who hold back delight in becoming (Iti 49).
Craving for annihilation, the third craving (SN 56.11); those repelled by becoming who delight in non-becoming 'overreach' (Iti 49).
Four kinds: clinging to sensual pleasures, views, rules and observances, and a doctrine of self (SN 12.2; MN 11); also the 'fuel' by which a fire burns, used of the aggregates.
Sensual, form and formless becoming, conditioned by clinging and conditioning birth (SN 12.2); 'the cessation of becoming is nibbāna' (SN 12.68).
'The cessation of becoming is nibbāna' — seen clearly by Nārada without yet being touched with the body (SN 12.68).
The birth of beings, their coming to be, the manifestation of the aggregates, the obtaining of the sense bases (SN 12.2); 'birth is ended' marks liberation.
Decay, brokenness, greying and wrinkling, and the passing away, death and laying down of the body (SN 12.2); the last link, conditioned by birth.

The supporting condition in the series from suffering through faith, gladness, rapture, tranquillity, happiness, concentration, knowledge and vision, disenchantment and dispassion to liberation and the knowledge of destruction (SN 12.23).

The four nutriments that maintain beings: edible food, contact, mental volition and consciousness (MN 9; SN 12.63); also the conditions that feed or starve the hindrances and awakening factors (SN 46.51).
The third factor (with the parents' union and the mother's season) needed for conception (MN 38); the commentaries read it as the being about to enter the womb.

Intention (cetanā): 'having intended, one acts by body, speech and mind' (AN 6.63); beings are owners and heirs of their deeds (MN 135); kamma ripens in this life, the next or later (AN 3.34; AN 6.63) and is one of the four unthinkables in its details (AN 4.77); four kinds, dark, bright, mixed and neither, the last leading to kamma's end (AN 4.232).

equivalents.note: same word; the suttas define kamma as intention and reject its identification with ritual action or with fate

definitions.definition: 'It is intention that I call kamma' (AN 6.63); one of the four nutriments (mental volition) and a component of name (SN 12.2).
The fruit of kamma, experienced in this life, the next or later (AN 6.63); the same deed ripens heavily or lightly depending on the doer's development (AN 3.100).
'Beings are owners of their deeds, heirs of their deeds; deeds are their womb, kin and refuge' (MN 135); one of the five reflections (AN 5.57).
The ten unwholesome courses (three bodily, four verbal, three mental) and their opposites (MN 41; AN 10.176).
The ending of kamma through the volition to abandon dark, bright and mixed kamma (AN 4.232–233).
The five destinations: hell, animal realm, ghost realm, humans, gods (MN 12).
The round of rebirth without discoverable beginning, in which more tears have been shed than the water of the four oceans (SN 15.3).
The world of the six senses: 'in this fathom-long body with its perception and mind I declare the world, its origin, cessation and the way' (SN 2.26); 'empty of self' (SN 35.85).
A cosmic period of contraction and expansion of the world (DN 27); the seven Buddhas arose within ninety-one aeons (DN 14).
The sectarian tenet that whatever one experiences is due to God's creation, rejected as leading to inaction (AN 3.61).

The destruction of greed, hatred and delusion (SN 38.1); the unconditioned (SN 43.12), the cessation of becoming (SN 12.68), the highest happiness (Dhp 203–204); described negatively as the sphere where there is no earth, water, fire, air … no coming or going (Ud 8.1) and as the unborn, unmade, unconditioned (Ud 8.3); named by many epithets (SN 43.44).
The one unconditioned dhamma, real and not mere absence, outside the aggregates; not a self (commentarial Theravāda).

equivalents.note: same word; whether anything is attained beyond the extinguishing (Brahman, self) is where the traditions differ; Theravāda rejects a self or ground

definitions.definition: The final passing of the Buddha or an arahant (DN 16), attained by the Buddha from the fourth jhāna; also used of full extinguishing of defilements in life.
Twofold: with residue remaining (the living arahant) and without residue remaining (at the arahant's death, when all that is felt becomes cool) (Iti 44).
The nibbāna-element of the arahant who still has the five faculties and experiences the agreeable and disagreeable (Iti 44).
The nibbāna-element in which all that is felt, not delighted in, becomes cool (Iti 44).
An epithet of nibbāna: the doors to the deathless are open (MN 26); heedfulness is the path to the deathless (Dhp 21); mindfulness of death merges in the deathless (AN 6.19).
What is not made by conditions: no arising, no passing, no alteration while standing is discerned (AN 3.47); the destruction of lust, hatred and delusion (SN 43.12).
What is made by conditions, with three marks: arising, passing away and alteration while standing (AN 3.47).
'There is an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned'; were there not, no escape from the born would be known (Ud 8.3; Iti 43).
The unsurpassed security from the yokes, nibbāna, sought in the noble search (MN 26).
The mind that has gone to the unconditioned has reached the destruction of cravings (Dhp 154); an epithet of nibbāna (SN 43).
In Dhp 154 the mind 'gone to visaṅkhāra' — read by the commentary as nibbāna.

Release of mind from the effluents: 'unshakeable is my liberation' (SN 56.11; MN 26); the fruit of disenchantment and dispassion (SN 22.59); with right knowledge it completes the ten factors of the arahant (MN 117).
Liberation of mind — immeasurable, through nothingness, emptiness, signless, and the unshakeable (MN 43); with liberation by wisdom, the arahant's attainment (AN 3.33).
Liberation of mind through wisdom, destroying the effluents; paired with liberation of mind (AN 3.33; MN 70).
The one taste of this Dhamma and discipline, as the ocean has the one taste of salt (Ud 5.5).
Turning away from the aggregates when seen as impermanent, suffering and not-self; leads to dispassion and liberation (SN 22.59; SN 12.23).
The fading away of lust that follows disenchantment and leads to liberation (SN 22.59); an epithet of nibbāna (SN 43.44).

Conventional designation: 'as the word chariot is used when parts are assembled, so the convention being when aggregates exist' (SN 5.10); the world's usages the Tathāgata uses without grasping (DN 9); later the conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) of the commentaries.

equivalents.note: the Madhyamaka two-truths term; the Pali commentaries' sammuti-sacca is close but not identical

definitions.definition: In the ultimate sense (paramatthato) no person is found (Mil 3.1.1); in the commentaries paramattha-sacca and the four ultimate realities (citta, cetasika, rūpa, nibbāna).
The conventional person: 'the bearer of the burden is the person' (SN 22.22); the seven and eight noble persons (MN 70); in the ultimate sense not found (Mil 3.1.1).
A conventional designation for the aggregates, as 'chariot' for its parts; 'no being is found here' (SN 5.10).
The five aggregates of clinging (MN 44).
Regarding form (and each aggregate) as self, self as having form, form in self or self in form — twenty kinds (MN 44); the first fetter, abandoned at stream-entry.
Conceiving things as self, in self, from self or as 'mine' (MN 1); 'I am' is a conceiving, a disease, a tumour, a dart (MN 140).

The proliferation of concepts that follows feeling, perception and thought, by which 'perceptions and notions tinged with proliferation' beset a person (MN 18); rooted in the thought 'I am' (Snp 4.14); the Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation (AN 8.30).

equivalents.note: same word; in Vedānta prapañca is the manifest world, in the suttas the mind's proliferation

definitions.definition: Freedom from proliferation, an epithet of nibbāna (SN 43.44) and the eighth thought of the great person (AN 8.30).

The residual conceit and desire 'I am' in one who no longer takes any aggregate as self, like the smell of soap in a washed cloth (SN 22.89); abandoned by the perception of impermanence (MN 62; Ud 4.1).
Conceit — 'I am better, equal, worse' (Snp 4.9); the eighth fetter, abandoned only at arahantship.
The making of 'I' and 'mine' and the underlying tendency to conceit, absent in the liberated one (AN 3.33).

equivalents.note: same word ahaṃkāra; in Sāṃkhya a cosmic evolute, here the mental act of I-making

definitions.definition: Latent tendencies — to sensual lust, aversion, views, doubt, conceit, lust for becoming and ignorance (MN 18); lust underlies pleasant feeling, aversion painful, ignorance neutral (MN 44; MN 148).
A view or theory, especially the speculative views (the sixty-two of DN 1, the ten undeclared of MN 72) that are 'a thicket, a fetter of views'; right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) is the first path factor.
The view that self and world are eternal (DN 1).
The view that the self is annihilated at death (DN 1; SN 44.10).
The questions the Buddha set aside (world eternal or not, finite or not, soul same as body or not, Tathāgata after death in four ways) because not beneficial (MN 63; MN 72; SN 44.10).

The mind that changes day and night like a monkey (SN 12.61); luminous but defiled by adventitious defilements (AN 1.51–52); to be tamed (Dhp 35); the third establishment of mindfulness; also an iddhipāda (concentration through mind).

notes: Shared slug with Yoga's citta; this is the early-Buddhist contribution.

definitions.definition: The sixth internal base, cognising mental objects; 'mind is the forerunner of all states' (Dhp 1–2).

equivalents.note: same word; in the suttas the sixth sense, not an evolute of prakṛti

definitions.definition: 'This mind is luminous, but defiled by adventitious defilements' — understood by the noble disciple, for whom there is development of mind (AN 1.51–52).
The sixteen defilements of mind (MN 7); the adventitious defilements of the luminous mind (AN 1.51); the imperfections of concentration (MN 128).
Greed, hatred, delusion and the states born of them (a mostly commentarial collective term).

equivalents.note: same word; the Yoga Sūtra's kleśas are a fivefold set (avidyā, asmitā, rāga, dveṣa, abhiniveśa)

definitions.definition: The effluents of sensuality, becoming and ignorance (MN 9; DN 2), with views as a fourth in some lists; their destruction is arahantship.

equivalents.note: same word; in Jainism āsrava is the influx of karmic matter

definitions.definition: The third true knowledge and sixth direct knowledge: knowing the four truths and the effluents, the mind is freed and knows 'birth is ended' (DN 2; MN 4).
The first unwholesome root (MN 9); a source for the origination of kamma (AN 3.34).
Lust, one of the three fires (SN 35.28); its destruction is part of nibbāna (SN 38.1).
The second unwholesome root (MN 9), one of the three fires (SN 35.28).
The third unwholesome root (MN 9), one of the three fires (SN 35.28).

Thought directed to an object; thoughts of sensuality, ill will and cruelty versus renunciation, good will and harmlessness (MN 19); verbal formation (MN 44); a factor of the first jhāna; removed by the five methods (MN 20).

equivalents.note: same word; the Yoga Sūtra uses it for the first level of samprajñāta samādhi

definitions.definition: Keeping the mind connected to its object; with vitakka the verbal formation (MN 44) and a factor of the first jhāna.
Attention, a component of name (SN 12.2) and a factor defined in each jhāna (MN 111).

Attention that goes to the source: by it effluents do not arise and are abandoned (MN 2); one of the two conditions for right view (MN 43) and a factor of stream-entry (SN 55.5); the bodhisatta's means of penetrating dependent origination (DN 14).
Unification of mind, which is concentration (MN 44); a factor of the jhānas (MN 111).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: The training of the higher mind (the jhānas) (AN 3.89); pursued by removing distracting thoughts (MN 20) and gross to subtle impurities (AN 3.101).
The acquisitions (aggregates, sensual objects, defilements) on which suffering depends (Ud 3.10); their relinquishing is nibbāna.

Abstention from killing, stealing, unchastity or sexual misconduct, false and harsh speech and the rest (DN 2); the first training, which purifies wisdom as wisdom purifies it (DN 4); its purpose is non-remorse (AN 11.1).

Unification of mind (MN 44); right concentration is the four jhānas (SN 45.8); noble right concentration is supported by the other seven path factors (MN 117); four developments of concentration (AN 4.41).

notes: Shared slug with the Yoga and Vedānta term; this is the early-Buddhist contribution.

definitions.definition: Understanding of the four truths and of rise and fall (SN 48.10); conjoined with consciousness (MN 43); the third training; born of meditation (Dhp 282), inseparable from jhāna (Dhp 372).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: The three trainings in higher virtue, higher mind and higher wisdom (AN 3.89); the training rules (sikkhāpada).
The training in higher virtue: restraint by the Pātimokkha, seeing danger in the slightest fault (AN 3.89).
The training in higher wisdom: knowing the four truths as they are (AN 3.89).

The four meditative absorptions: the first with applied and sustained thought, rapture and bliss born of seclusion; the second with rapture and bliss born of concentration; the third with bliss and equanimity; the fourth with purity of mindfulness through equanimity (DN 2; SN 45.8); remembered by the bodhisatta as 'the path to awakening' (MN 36); a basis for destroying the effluents (AN 9.36).

equivalents.note: same word; the Pali jhāna is a specific fourfold absorption, Yoga's dhyāna the seventh limb

definitions.definition: Rapture born of seclusion or concentration, factor of the first two jhānas (DN 2); the fourth factor of awakening; arises from gladness and leads to tranquillity (SN 12.23).
The bliss of the first three jhānas (DN 2); the pleasure the bodhisatta saw no reason to fear (MN 36); nibbāna is the highest happiness (Dhp 203–204).

Equanimity: the fourth brahmavihāra (abandoning aversion, MN 62), the seventh factor of awakening, the purity of the fourth jhāna; equanimity based on unity abandons that based on diversity (MN 137); the tenth perfection (Bv 2).

equivalents.note: same word; YS 1.33 lists it among the four attitudes

definitions.definition: Calming of body and mind; the fifth factor of awakening; arising from rapture and leading to happiness (SN 12.23; MN 118).
Gladness arising from faith or from non-remorse, leading to rapture (SN 12.23; AN 11.1).
Freedom from remorse, the purpose of wholesome virtue and the basis of gladness (AN 11.1).
Calm of mind, developed with insight (MN 43; MN 149); the path to the unconditioned (SN 43.12); calm preceding, following or yoked with insight (AN 4.170).
Clear seeing into states as they are — their rise and fall, impermanence and not-self (MN 131; AN 4.170); paired with calm (MN 149).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: Mindfulness of in- and out-breathing in sixteen steps, which fulfils the four establishments of mindfulness, the seven factors of awakening, and true knowledge and liberation (MN 118; SN 54.1).
In-and-out breathing (MN 44), calmed in the fourth step of mindfulness of breathing (MN 118).
Perception and feeling (MN 44), experienced and calmed in the second tetrad of mindfulness of breathing (MN 118).
Acting with full awareness when going and returning, looking, bending, eating, speaking and keeping silent (DN 2; MN 10).
Guarding the doors of the senses: seeing a form one does not grasp at its signs and features through which covetousness and grief might invade (DN 2; MN 27).
Contentment with robes and alms-food, like a bird with its wings (DN 2); 'contentment is the greatest wealth' (Dhp 204).
The path to the deathless (Dhp 21); the Buddha's last words urge accomplishing the goal through heedfulness (DN 16).
The inner sense of shame that, with ottappa, protects the world; the first quality of a true ascetic (MN 39).
Regard for consequences and for others' blame, paired with hiri (MN 39).
Patient endurance of abuse and injury (MN 21; MN 145); the sixth perfection (Bv 2).
The effacement of defilements by forty-four resolves; the jhānas are 'peaceful abidings', not effacement (MN 8).
Seclusion of body and mind; the first jhāna is born of seclusion (DN 2); a monk who delights in company cannot reach liberation of mind (MN 122).
Spiritual friendship, 'the whole of the holy life' (SN 45.2); the first condition for maturing the liberation of mind (Ud 4.1).
Confidence in the Tathāgata's awakening (SN 48.10), placed after examining a teacher (MN 95; MN 47); faith arises from suffering and leads to gladness (SN 12.23); the first faculty and power.

equivalents.note: same word; YS 1.20 lists śraddhā first among the five means

definitions.definition: Unshakeable confidence in the Buddha, Dhamma and Saṅgha, with the virtues dear to the noble ones — the mirror of the Dhamma of the stream-enterer (DN 16).
Energy, to be balanced like lute strings (AN 6.55); the faculty of energy is the four right strivings (SN 48.10); a factor of awakening, an iddhipāda and the fifth perfection.

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: Mindfulness established in the four satipaṭṭhānas (MN 10); the faculty of mindfulness (SN 48.10); the first factor of awakening, always useful (SN 46.53); dams the currents of the world (Snp 5.2).

equivalents.note: same word; smṛti in the Brahmanical traditions also means remembered tradition

definitions.definition: The four establishments of mindfulness — contemplating body, feelings, mind and dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and grief (MN 10); the direct path to purification and nibbāna; one's own pasture (SN 47.6).
The seven factors: mindfulness, investigation of dhammas, energy, rapture, tranquillity, concentration, equanimity (MN 118; SN 46.51–53).

equivalents.note: same term

definitions.definition: The second factor of awakening, investigating states with wisdom; to be aroused when the mind is sluggish (SN 46.53).
The five spiritual faculties — faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom (SN 48.10); also the six sense faculties, to be developed not by blindness but by equanimity (MN 152).
Concentration due to desire, energy, mind or investigation, with formations of striving (SN 51.20); for a monk, 'long life' (DN 26).
Wholesome desire to act, the first basis of power (SN 51.20); in 'kāmacchanda' sensual desire.
The fourth basis of power, concentration through investigation (SN 51.20).
The many kinds of power — becoming many, passing through walls, walking on water, flying, touching sun and moon (DN 2); the first direct knowledge; its display is disparaged as a 'wonder' (DN 11).

equivalents.note: the Yoga and haṭha texts' siddhis overlap with the iddhis; the suttas treat display of them as unfit

definitions.definition: Six direct knowledges: psychic power, divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, the divine eye, destruction of the effluents (DN 2; MN 119).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: Seeing beings passing away and reappearing according to their deeds (DN 2; MN 4); the second true knowledge.
Recollecting one's many past births with their details (DN 2; MN 4); the first true knowledge.
A body created from this body, complete in its limbs, drawn out like a reed from its sheath (DN 2).

Recollection of past lives, the divine eye and the destruction of the effluents, attained on the night of awakening (MN 4; MN 36) — the Buddhist re-definition of the brahmin's 'three Vedas' (DN 13; AN 3.58).
The three knowledges; 'ignorance was destroyed and knowledge arose' (MN 4); with liberation, the fruit of the awakening factors (MN 118).
One accomplished in knowledge and conduct is best among gods and humans (DN 3; DN 27); the gradual training (conduct) and the knowledges.
Knowledge and vision of the body and consciousness (DN 2); of things as they are (SN 12.23); of liberation.
The three wonders of psychic power, mind-reading and instruction, of which only instruction is praised (DN 11).
The ten powers of knowledge by which the Tathāgata roars the lion's roar (MN 12).
The Tathāgata's four grounds of fearlessness (MN 12).

The attainment of cessation beyond the formless spheres, in which verbal, bodily and mental formations cease but vitality and heat remain (MN 43; MN 44); reached progressively 'with full awareness' (DN 9).
The first formless attainment, reached by passing beyond perceptions of form (MN 121; MN 111).
The second formless attainment (MN 121; MN 111).
The third formless attainment, taught to the bodhisatta by Āḷāra Kālāma (MN 26); Upasīva is told to cross the flood relying on nothingness (Snp 5.7).
The fourth formless attainment, taught by Uddaka Rāmaputta (MN 26); not leading to nibbāna by itself.
The signless concentration and liberation of mind, empty of the 'makers of signs' lust, hatred and delusion (MN 43; MN 121).
Emptiness as a dwelling — what is absent is seen as empty and what remains as present (MN 121); the world is empty of self and what belongs to self (SN 35.85); emptiness concentration (SN 43.12).

equivalents.note: same word; Madhyamaka universalises emptiness as absence of own-nature

definitions.definition: Empty of self or what belongs to self (SN 35.85); 'look upon the world as empty' (Snp 5.16).
Not being 'made of that', by which even equanimity based on unity is abandoned (MN 137).
Ten kasiṇas — earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, white, space, consciousness — perceived above, below, across, non-dual, immeasurable (AN 10.25).
Recollection of death, 'may I live for one breath', of great fruit, merging in the deathless (AN 6.19).
The sign of reviewing, well grasped, like one standing who looks at one seated — the fifth factor of noble right concentration (AN 5.28).
The four floods (sensual pleasure, becoming, views, ignorance) crossed 'without halting and without straining' (SN 1.1; SN 35.238).
'Live as islands to yourselves, with the Dhamma as island' (DN 16; SN 47.13); nibbāna is 'the island' (SN 43.44).
The Tathāgata has no closed fist of a teacher holding back teachings (DN 16).
The four great references by which a claimed teaching is checked against the discourses and the discipline (DN 16).
What the Buddha taught; checked by the great references (DN 16); for Theravāda the Tipiṭaka as recited at the First Council.
'Not doing any evil, undertaking the wholesome, purifying one's mind: this is the teaching of the Buddhas' (Dhp 183).

The Buddha's teaching, well proclaimed, visible here and now (AN 6.10); what is seen by seeing dependent origination (MN 28); also any phenomenon ('all dhammas are not-self'), a mental object (the fourth satipaṭṭhāna) and a quality.

equivalents.note: same word; the Brahmanical dharma is primarily duty and cosmic order

definitions.definition: The teaching and the monastic discipline together, the Teacher after the Buddha's passing (DN 16); like the ocean with eight wonders (Ud 5.5).
The dust-free eye of Dhamma: 'whatever is subject to arising is subject to cessation' — stream-entry (SN 56.11; Vin Mv 1.23).
The code of rules (227 for monks, 311 for nuns) recited on the uposatha; restraint by it is the training in higher virtue (AN 3.89).
Restraint by the Pātimokkha as the first step of the gradual training (DN 2; MN 107).
The monastic discipline laid down for ten reasons (Vin Pār 1) and recited by Upāli at the First Council (Cv 11).
The eight principles of respect accepted by Mahāpajāpatī as her ordination (Cv 10.1.4; AN 8.51).
Leaving the household life for homelessness (DN 2); the going forth of a slave brings the first visible fruit of the contemplative life (DN 2).
Jhāna, knowledge and vision, the paths and fruits; falsely claiming one entails defeat (Vin Pār 4).
A text recited for protection: the Āṭānāṭiya verses (DN 32), the Ratana and Mettā suttas; the tradition's chanted protection.
A solemn declaration of truth by which a result is brought about — Aṅgulimāla's for a woman in labour (MN 86); the refrain of the Ratana Sutta.
Going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, three times (Khp 1); first used as ordination (Vin Mv 1.12).
Sacrifice re-interpreted: a bloodless offering, then giving, dwellings, refuge, precepts, going forth and knowledge as sacrifices of greater fruit (DN 5).

equivalents.note: same word; the Buddha redefines sacrifice and rejects animal offerings; the Vedic tradition holds its own account

definitions.definition: Self-mortification, one of the two extremes (SN 56.11); the bodhisatta's extreme austerities did not lead to awakening (MN 12, MN 36); re-used as 'restraint' in Snp 1.4 and Snp 2.4.

equivalents.note: same word; Jain and Brahmanical traditions value tapas as purifying

definitions.definition: A wandering renunciant; true ascetics are found only where the eightfold path is (DN 16; MN 11); one becomes an ascetic by the calming of evil (Dhp 265).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: Re-defined by conduct: one is a brahmin not by birth but by deeds (MN 98; Snp 1.7); 'him I call a brahmin who has nothing and takes nothing' (Dhp 396); the arahant as the true brahmin.

equivalents.note: same word; the Brahmanical tradition defines it primarily by birth

definitions.definition: The four classes (khattiya, brāhmaṇa, vessa, sudda), which arose from occupations (DN 27) and are all capable of purity (MN 93).

equivalents.note: same word; its basis (birth versus conduct) is disputed

definitions.definition: One is an outcaste by deeds, not by birth (Snp 1.7).
The sage at peace, not born, not ageing, not dying, beyond conceiving (MN 140); the sage of the Aṭṭhakavagga who holds no views (Snp 4).
The Buddha's term for himself and for the liberated one, who cannot be described as existing, not existing, both or neither after death, being deep like the ocean (MN 72; SN 22.86).

literal: the one thus gone / thus come

definitions.definition: One who has awakened: 'remember me as a Buddha', neither god, gandhabba, yakkha nor human (AN 4.36).
Supreme perfect awakening, claimed only when knowledge of the four truths in three turnings and twelve aspects was purified (SN 56.11).
The Buddha before his awakening ('when I was still a bodhisatta', MN 4, MN 19, MN 36); the norms of a bodhisatta (DN 14); Sumedha's aspiration (Bv 2).

equivalents.note: same word; in the Nikāyas the Buddha-to-be, in the Mahāyāna an ideal for all

definitions.definition: One who awakens by himself but does not found a teaching; the Khaggavisāṇa verses are traditionally ascribed to them (Snp 1.3, commentary).
Sumedha's aspiration to Buddhahood, which succeeds by the combination of eight conditions (Bv 2.59).
The ten perfections fulfilled by a bodhisatta — giving, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, equanimity (Bv 2.116–165).

equivalents.note: Mahāyāna lists six or ten pāramitās with different members

definitions.definition: Giving, the first ground of merit and first perfection (Bv 2); regular giving is a sacrifice of great fruit (DN 5).
Renunciation of sensual pleasure; the third perfection (Bv 2); thoughts of renunciation (MN 19).
The eighth perfection, unshakeable like a rocky mountain (Bv 2); the four foundations of MN 140 (wisdom, truth, relinquishment, peace).
Truth: the four noble truths; the seventh perfection (Bv 2); the preservation of truth (MN 95).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: Love, compassion, rejoicing and equanimity pervading all directions boundlessly — the path to companionship with Brahmā (DN 13); 'a divine abiding here' (Snp 1.8).
The four immeasurables (brahmavihāras) and the immeasurable liberation of mind (MN 43).

A boundless mind of love for all beings, as a mother for her only child (Snp 1.8); kept even under the saw (MN 21); its liberation of mind has eleven benefits (AN 11.15) and outshines all merit (Iti 27).

equivalents.note: same word; YS 1.33 lists maitrī among the four attitudes

definitions.definition: The second brahmavihāra, abandoning cruelty (MN 62; DN 13).

notes: Shared slug with the Sanskrit term.

definitions.definition: The third brahmavihāra, abandoning discontent (MN 62; DN 13).

notes: Shared slug with the Sanskrit term.

definitions.definition: 'Hatred is appeased by non-hatred: this is an eternal law' (Dhp 5; Vin Mv 10.2).
The uninstructed ordinary person who perceives and conceives (MN 1) and feels two darts (SN 36.6).
A noble disciple in training (stream-enterer to one on the path of arahantship), who should not conceive (MN 1).
The stream is the noble eightfold path (SN 55.5).
One who possesses the noble eightfold path (SN 55.5), has the eye of Dhamma, has abandoned identity view, doubt and clinging to rules and vows, and is no longer bound for the lower realms (DN 16).
One who, with the three fetters abandoned and lust, hatred and delusion attenuated, returns to this world only once more.
One who has abandoned the five lower fetters and is reborn spontaneously in the pure abodes, attaining nibbāna there without returning (MN 64; MN 10).
One whose effluents are destroyed, who has lived the holy life and done what was to be done (DN 2); has ten factors (MN 117).

equivalents.note: same word

definitions.definition: A non-returner whose mind is not bound to sensual pleasures (Thig 1.12).
One who contacts the formless liberations with the body and has destroyed the effluents by wisdom (MN 70; DN 15).
One whose effluents are destroyed by wisdom without contacting the formless liberations (MN 70).
A trainee who contacts the formless liberations and has some effluents destroyed (MN 70).
A trainee who has understood and reviewed the teaching with wisdom (MN 70).
A trainee whose faith in the Tathāgata is settled (MN 70).
One on the path to stream-entry who accepts the teachings after pondering them with wisdom (MN 70).
One on the path to stream-entry who has faith and love for the Tathāgata (MN 70).
The noble, taintless path factors, as distinct from the mundane ones affected by the effluents (MN 117).
Final knowledge (arahantship) in this life, one of the two fruits of satipaṭṭhāna (MN 10).
The pleasure in sensual pleasures, forms and feelings (MN 13).
The danger in sensual pleasures — toil, loss, conflict, bad destiny (MN 13).
The removal of desire and lust for what gratifies (MN 13).
The five cords of sensual pleasure (MN 26); like the sores of a leper (MN 75); gratification, danger and escape (MN 13).
Forms, sounds, odours, tastes and tangibles that are desirable, enticing (MN 26).
The four biases by which evil is done: desire, hatred, delusion, fear (DN 31).
'Of things that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has told the cause and their cessation' (Vin Mv 1.23).
'Delight is the root of suffering' (MN 1); delight and lust are the hidden assassin (SN 35.238).
Taking the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, not-self as self and the unattractive as attractive (AN 4.49).
The four unthinkables: the Buddhas' domain, jhāna's domain, the results of kamma, speculation about the world (AN 4.77).
Vitality, on which the five faculties depend and which depends on heat (MN 43).
Bodily heat, which with vitality and consciousness leaves the body at death (MN 43; SN 22.95).
The seven purifications of virtue, mind, view, overcoming doubt, knowledge of path and not-path, knowledge of the way, and knowledge and vision, each like a chariot in a relay (MN 24).
In Dhp 282 'from yoga wisdom arises' — application in meditation; also the four yokes (sensuality, becoming, views, ignorance).

notes: Slug suffixed to keep the Pali sense apart from trm:yoga (Pātañjala).

definitions.definition: The thirty-seven qualities in seven groups — four establishments of mindfulness, four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of awakening, the noble eightfold path — taught for the long duration of the holy life (DN 16; MN 149).

Contemplating the body in the body — breathing, postures, clear comprehension, the parts, the elements, the charnel-ground stages (MN 10). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four establishments of mindfulness.

Knowing pleasant, painful and neutral feelings, worldly and unworldly (MN 10). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four establishments of mindfulness.

Knowing the mind as with or without lust, hatred, delusion, contracted or scattered, exalted, concentrated, liberated (MN 10). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four establishments of mindfulness.

Contemplating the hindrances, aggregates, sense bases, awakening factors and the four truths (MN 10; DN 22). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four establishments of mindfulness.

Generating desire and effort so that unarisen unwholesome states do not arise (SN 45.8; DN 33). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four right efforts.
Generating desire and effort to abandon arisen unwholesome states (SN 45.8). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four right efforts.
Generating desire and effort so that unarisen wholesome states arise (SN 45.8). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four right efforts.

Generating desire and effort to maintain and increase arisen wholesome states (SN 45.8). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four right efforts.
Concentration due to desire with formations of striving (SN 51.20). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four bases of power.
Concentration due to energy with formations of striving (SN 51.20). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four bases of power.
Concentration due to mind with formations of striving (SN 51.20). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four bases of power.
Concentration due to investigation with formations of striving (SN 51.20). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four bases of power.
Faith in the Tathāgata's awakening (SN 48.10). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five faculties.
The four right strivings (SN 48.10). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five faculties.
The four establishments of mindfulness (SN 48.10). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five faculties.
The four jhānas, made with relinquishment as object (SN 48.10). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five faculties.
Noble penetrative wisdom into rise and fall (SN 48.10). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five faculties.
Faith as a power unshaken by faithlessness (SN 50). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five powers.
Energy as a power unshaken by laziness (SN 50). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five powers.
Mindfulness as a power unshaken by heedlessness (SN 50). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five powers.
Concentration as a power unshaken by distraction (SN 50). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five powers.
Wisdom as a power unshaken by ignorance (SN 50). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the five powers.
Mindfulness established, always useful (MN 118; SN 46.53). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the seven factors of awakening.

Investigating states with wisdom; nourished by attending to wholesome and unwholesome states (SN 46.51). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the seven factors of awakening.

Unflagging energy; nourished by the elements of arousal, exertion and endeavour (SN 46.51). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the seven factors of awakening.
Spiritual rapture arising in one who has aroused energy (MN 118). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the seven factors of awakening.

Tranquillity of body and mind (MN 118); to be developed when the mind is restless (SN 46.53). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the seven factors of awakening.
The concentration of one tranquil and happy (MN 118). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the seven factors of awakening.
Looking on with equanimity at the concentrated mind (MN 118). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the seven factors of awakening.

Knowledge of the four truths (SN 45.8); understanding the wholesome and its roots (MN 9); mundane and supramundane, and first of the factors (MN 117). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the noble eightfold path.
Intention of renunciation, non-ill-will and harmlessness (SN 45.8; MN 19). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the noble eightfold path.

Abstaining from false, divisive, harsh speech and idle chatter (SN 45.8); speaking only the true and beneficial at the right time (MN 58). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the noble eightfold path.
Abstaining from killing, stealing and sexual misconduct (SN 45.8). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the noble eightfold path.

Abandoning wrong livelihood (SN 45.8) — for lay followers the five wrong trades (AN 5.177). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the noble eightfold path.
The four right strivings (SN 45.8). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the noble eightfold path.
The four establishments of mindfulness (SN 45.8). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the noble eightfold path.

The four jhānas (SN 45.8); unification supported by the other seven factors (MN 117); five-factored (AN 5.28). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the noble eightfold path.
The five powers — faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom — the faculties become unshakeable; one of the seven groups of the thirty-seven qualities.
The four right strivings (restraint, abandoning, developing, maintaining), identical with right effort (SN 45.8); one of the seven groups of the thirty-seven.

The five hindrances — sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, doubt — which obstruct the mind, like debt, disease, prison, slavery and a desert crossing (DN 2), or like dyed, boiling, mossy, windswept and muddy water (SN 46.55).
The first hindrance, fed by unwise attention to the sign of the beautiful and starved by attention to the sign of foulness (SN 46.51).
The second hindrance, fed by attention to the sign of the repulsive and starved by the liberation of mind by love (SN 46.51).
The third hindrance, fed by discontent, lethargy and sleepiness after meals and starved by arousal and exertion (SN 46.51; AN 7.61).
The fourth hindrance, fed by unsettledness of mind and starved by peace of mind (SN 46.51).
The fifth hindrance and second fetter, fed by things that are the basis for doubt and starved by wise attention to wholesome and unwholesome states (SN 46.51).

The ten fetters: five lower (identity view, doubt, clinging to rules and vows, sensual lust, ill will) and five higher (lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, ignorance) (MN 64).
The third fetter: taking rules and vows as themselves purifying (MN 2; MN 64).
The fourth fetter, abandoned by the non-returner (MN 64).
Ill will as the fifth fetter (MN 64).
Lust for existence in the form realm; the sixth fetter.
Lust for existence in the formless realm; the seventh fetter.
Restlessness as the ninth fetter and part of the fourth hindrance.
The task regarding the first truth: suffering is to be fully understood (SN 56.11).
The task regarding the second truth: its origin, craving, is to be abandoned (SN 56.11); also the second right effort.
The task regarding the third truth: cessation is to be realised (SN 56.11).

The task regarding the fourth truth: the path is to be developed (SN 56.11); the development of mind (cittabhāvanā) possible for one who understands the luminous mind (AN 1.52); development of concentration (AN 4.41) and of the faculties (MN 152).

notes: Shared slug with the Sanskrit term; this is the early-Buddhist contribution.

definitions.definition: Language or dialect: the Buddha allows his word to be learned 'in one's own language' (sakāya niruttiyā) and forbids putting it into Vedic metre (Vin Cv 5.33); analytical knowledge of language is one of the four paṭisambhidās.
